newsitem.title: UK: Darling refuses to commit UK Labour on public pay.
newsitem.headline: Darling refuses to commit UK Labour on public pay.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour Party is committed to tight spending control if it wins power and is not prepared to make pay pledges to public-sector workers that it cannot keep, finance spokesman Alistair Darling said.

"We are not going to get ourselves into a position of making commitments, making promises that may not be deliverable because of the true state of the public finances," Darling, the shadow chief secretary to the treasury, told BBC radio on Tuesday.

He was commenting on Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke's recommendation to the Pay Review Bodies, which cover 1.3 million public sector staff, that 1997 wage rises should be lower than in 1996 and that and increases should be met out of efficiency savings.

"We will maintain tight control of public spending. It's absolutely essential to do that if we're going to get the sort of stability on which we're going to build a sustainable economic success in the future," Darling said.
He said Clarke's tough line on pay would make it difficult to retain and motivate staff such as teachers and nurses who form the backbone of the economy.
But asked whether public-sector workers should therefore expect to be paid more by a Labour government, Darling replied: "Anyone proceeding on that assumption will be doing so on a false basis."

Darling said Labour would make its spending decisions once it had made a thorough assessment of the state of Britain's finances, which he said he suspected were in poorer shape than portrayed by Clarke.

"To start with, most people understand that any government has got to keep a proper control of public finances and we have no intention of giving in or surrendering positions that cannot be justified and cannot be paid for," Darling said.
